questions.question: Describe how this practice run distributes its marks across question shapes — quick-fire objective work, short answers, data questions, paragraph answers and the essay — and explain the strategy of matching effort to marks that the session trains.
questions.expected_answer: The practice set opens with thirty marks of quick-fire objective work: multiple-choice items at two marks, matching items at one, and give-the-term items at one, where abbreviations and shortened forms earn nothing. Longer questions open with four marks of short answers — two one-mark naming items and one two-mark application item answered in a single line of cause and consequence. Data questions carry ten marks each and climb from one-mark read-offs through two-mark descriptions to four-mark explanations or calculations, always marked as two marks per developed fact. Paragraph answers carry ten marks — five developed facts at two marks each, with a verbal graph able to stand in for one fact — and the essay carries thirty, split as definition 2, main body 20, evaluation 6 and closing judgement 2. The strategy: the mark value is the instruction. A two-mark answer is one or two lines, never a paragraph; a four-mark calculation needs its setup line, workings and labelled answer; a paragraph needs its facts counted before writing; and choices between questions are made by the friendliness of the data, since data questions and paragraphs carry the weight of the marks.

questions.question: Using the practice table — goods exports 950, net gold exports 150, services receipts 300, income receipts 100, merchandise imports 1 250, payments for services 180, income payments 220, current transfers plus 30 — calculate the trade balance and the balance on the current account in full marking style, and suggest two corrective measures for the result.
questions.expected_answer: Trade balance = goods exports + net gold exports − merchandise imports = 950 + 150 − 1 250 = −150 million, a trade deficit. Balance on current account: total receipts = 950 + 150 + 300 + 100 = 1 500; total payments = 1 250 + 180 + 220 = 1 650; 1 500 − 1 650 = −150; plus net current transfers of +30 gives −120 million — a deficit on the current account. Full marks require the setup line naming the items, the intermediate totals, and the final answer labelled with its sign, its units and its name, because a naked number forfeits the method marks. Corrective measures, each developed with its mechanism: raise interest rates to attract foreign capital into the financial account, which finances the deficit; promote exports through incentives and trade missions so receipts grow; allow the exchange rate to depreciate so imports become dearer and exports more competitive abroad; or manage import spending within the limits that trade agreements allow. Any two, explained, earn the follow-up marks.

questions.question: Plan this session's thirty-mark practice essay 'Discuss how monetary and fiscal policy can be used to smooth out business cycles, and evaluate how well these demand-side policies work', naming what earns the marks in each structural part.
questions.expected_answer: Definition opening (2): business cycles are the repeating expansions and contractions of economic activity around a long-term trend — a clean definition with no borrowed question wording and no announcement of the plan. Main body (20), with every fact tied to smoothing since an unlinked fact earns one mark instead of two: monetary policy in the downswing — the central bank cuts the repo rate to cheapen credit and lift consumption and investment, buys securities to inject liquidity, and applies moral suasion; reversed in the upswing to cool excess demand. Fiscal policy in the downswing — higher government spending and lower taxes inject demand that the multiplier enlarges; in the upswing spending restraint and progressive taxation withdraw it; automatic stabilisers — progressive taxes and grants — adjust with income on their own. Verbal graph: aggregate demand shifts right under stimulus and left under restraint along aggregate supply. Evaluation (6): lags can land stimulus after the phase has passed; lower unemployment tends to cost higher inflation; the repo rate cannot fix supply shocks such as droughts or electricity failures; borrowed stimulus becomes tomorrow's interest bill; judgement — demand-side smoothing works moderately and belongs beside supply-side reform. Closing judgement (2): one fresh line, such as that smoothing succeeds when the policy mix matches the phase and the cause of the cycle, never a repeat of the body.
